newsitem.title: GERMANY: Siemens turns overseas for growth, workers.
newsitem.headline: Siemens turns overseas for growth, workers.

text.p: German industrial giant Siemens AG is turning away from the rising labour costs and sluggish economy in its home country to build bases for future growth in foreign markets.
Siemens said on Thursday it expected international business to generate 70 percent of sales within the next five years, up from 62 percent today.
At the same time, Siemens, one of Germany's largest employers, expected to add thousands of jobs overseas while limiting payrolls in Germany.
Although he did not say it directly, chief executive Heinrich von Pierer made it clear Germany's roll in the company's future is declining.
"In two years, more than half of our employees will be located outside of Germany for the first time," chief executive Heinrich von Pierer said at Siemens' annual news conference.
"Growth in fiscal 1996 was fuelled by double-digit increases in our international business," Pierer said. "Business in Germany, on the other hand, stagnated."
International orders rose 17 percent in 1995/96, and sales 14 percent, while German orders were flat and sales dipped.

The same trends were reflected in the makeup of Siemens workers. The company added 14,000 employees overseas, but cut 6,000 at home, and shed 2,000 more in the sale of its high-end printer business, Pierer said.
The company plans to cut another 6,000 domestic workers in 1996/97.

Wage increases and shorter work weeks negotiated with German unions caused domestic personnel costs to rise seven percent last year, adding 1.4 billion marks in costs, Pierer said. German sales fell four percent to 35.9 billion marks as international sales rose 14 eprcent to 50.9 billion marks boosted by gains of 30 percent gains in Asia and 20 percent in the United States.
For sales growth and future employees, Siemens is looking toward the same foreign markets, and jobs will follow.
"We will continue building up our local workforces and local content," Pierer said. "This will affect our overall employment structure."
